utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. I was told that the Prosecution has some update for documents which have now a translation. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone else. Yes, there are nine new translations have been updated and I think a paper has been distributed, but I can read through the relevant exhibit numbers, if Your Honours would like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful. If you can, without any explanation, just give the number -- oh, they all have already a P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that from the list. P1307, P1308, P1311, P1542C, P1542D, P1562C, P1563C, P1565B, and P1569C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They are now exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: One further matter, Your Honour, is that having sent an e-mail last night about the sequence of witnesses, starting with today's witness, today's witness is in fact indicated he has moved his meeting on Monday and is able to continue, if necessary, on Monday, so it will treat him as a normal witness, we don't need to break his testimony in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this information. If there is nothing further, we -- the witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Elderkin, in between, I have a question. In the list of witnesses for this week, there was an indication that David Wood would be as 92 ter witness. I think that should be a mistake. If I'm not mistaken, the witness is a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honour. I understand that a revised list was sent correcting that error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Here is the Bench; I am speaking. Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, for the Prosecution, has questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can I ask to briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: David John Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: British.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what's your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I'm currently a non-executive director of a number of companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what was your previous occupation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Previous to commerce or previous to my current position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Previous to commerce.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I was in the British Army for about 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And remind myself and for your information, because we're speaking the same language I'll try to leave a pause after I finish my question and if you could leave a pause as well. Could you tell us what years you served in the British Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I served from 1979 through to early 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what was your rank on your retirement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I retired as a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you serving in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: In 1995, I was serving in Bosnia as part of the United Nations Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what was your role?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I was in command of an organisation there known as the Joint Commission Observers, the JCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, briefly, what did your role and the role of the JCOs involve?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, the JCOs were an organisation that were set up to try and overcome some of the communication and verification issues that were beset UNPROFOR at the time, and I was the commander of the unit that was assigned to the role of -- of joint commission observer, so I was a major at the time and I had about 20 or 30 soldiers that were acting under my command as JCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you personally based?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I was personally based in Sarajevo and I was based in the residency there working directly for General Smith, who, at that stage, was the commander of UNPROFOR, and I had with me a small staff of Joint Commission Observers and I also had Joint Commission Observers who were out in the various trouble spots, if you like, in the various enclaves at the time who were reporting to me and I was able then to report to General Smith and to tell him what was going on and to provide a sort of focus for -- as I say, information, reporting, verification, and, indeed, sometimes often a negotiation of action on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you work closely with General Smith?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, very closely. I spoke with him every day, several times a day. I used to attend with him all of the various or certainly most of the various meetings he had with the senior leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, the Federation, the Bosnian Muslims, the Croats and so on. So I was with him -- I was with him for a large part much most days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible to move a little bit further to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Also ask that you try to speak a little bit slower so that the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who were the principle Bosnian Serb officials with whom you were dealing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I personally, of course, wasn't dealing with any of them. Well, that is not quite true, I suppose. Speaking personally then, I was dealing regularly with a Bosnian Serb army officer called Milenko Indjic, who was based at a barracks at Lukavica and who was the Bosnian Serb officer responsible for liaising with UNPROFOR, so I dealt with him personally frequently. But General Smith, of course, was dealing, and I was helping him deal, with everybody from Karadzic through Mladic, Tolimir, and down the chain, effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you meet then with some of the generals from the Bosnian Serb army on occasion?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Oh, yes, on occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us about -- starting from the top down, did you get to meet General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. I met General Mladic on several occasions, I would guess four or five in total, always with General Smith -- not always with General Smith. Usually with General Smith. On one occasion, with General Nicolai, who was the Dutch Chief of Staff. And, generally speaking, we met him for the purposes of meetings between Smith and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how about General named Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I am pretty sure I met him but I don't really remember him very clearly, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, I know I met him because I have seen a video of me in -- with him, but I don't really remember him very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how about General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I met General Tolimir several times with General Mladic and I have a clear recollection of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point I have to interrupt you. I would like to clarify one sentence, I'm not sure if that was recorded correctly. Page 6, lines 5 through 7, you are recorded as having said: "But General Smith, of course, was dealing, and I was helping him deal, with everybody from Karadzic through Mladic, Tolimir, and down the chain, effectively." Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is probably my fault for speaking too quickly again. What I was trying to say was that -- I was trying to differentiate between my own dealings with the Bosnian Serb authorities which was mainly confined to dealing with Indjic and General Smith's dealing which were, obviously, with Karadzic, Mladic, Tolimir, and so on. And I met with these Bosnian Serb generals as part of General Smith's entourage on several occasions. That was the point I was trying to make. I'm sorry if I didn't make it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In what circumstances did you first meet General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I first met General Tolimir at Pale on, I think, the 30th of April or thereabouts. When we went to Pale -- when I say "we" this was General Smith, his entourage, myself included, and Mr. Akashi at the time and his entourage, and we went to Pale to peak with Karadzic. And there was a joint press conference of some description there, and I met General Tolimir on that occasion. We had a lunch together and we had lunch all together. And I -- and I, in fact, I sat opposite General Tolimir during that lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did have you any opportunity to speak to him on that occasion or learn about his work?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. I was introduced to him. He either didn't speak English or didn't want to speak English, so it was a limited conversation since my Serbo-Croat is not extensive. But he clearly knew who I was, because he said to me at one point, You and me, we are in the same business. And I took that to mean that he recognised that I had a role that was linked to intelligence of some sort. He also took the opportunity to show me a little leather pouch he wore in his belt in which he had a grenade and he said something to the effect that, I carry this with me all the time. They will never take me alive because I will use this to kill myself if they do. So that was the sort of conversation we had. It wasn't a fluent conversation because we were sort of talking in different languages and a lot of it was by gesticulation and by a little bit of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you really to slow down while you're speaking. It is very difficult to catch everything for the interpreters and the court recorder and please pause between question and answer. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned that first meeting with General Tolimir was around the 30th of April. Could you just confirm for our written record what year?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what role did General Tolimir have during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: My understanding was that he was responsible for intelligence and security for the Bosnian Serb army. So my interpretation of that was that he was General Mladic's right-hand man, if you like, with regard to ensuring that Mladic knew all that he needed to know about what was going on in Bosnia, going on in UNPROFOR, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you attend any other meetings at which General Tolimir was present, other than the one around the 30th of April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. The next meeting that I can recollect meeting Tolimir at, was on around the 19th of July when we met at a restaurant which I've subsequently discovered was called the Jela restaurant, but at the time I don't think I was aware of its name. And at that meeting, Mladic was there, Tolimir was there, Smith was there, and Smith's entourage, including myself. And the purpose of that meeting was to sign an agreement between Mladic and Smith and obviously the rest of us were essentially helping in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Based on your observation, how was Tolimir's relationship with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: It seemed to me that there was a very close relationship between them. Certainly there appeared to be a mutual respect between them. And during the meeting of the 19th that I'm referring to, there was an occasion where General Tolimir was interrupting the process of forming the agreement and wanting to change little things in it. And General Smith made a joke to General Mladic and said words to the effect that, General Tolimir is what we in the British Army would call a military shit. And by that what he meant was he is a -- that he is a very picky officer, professional officer who wants to see everything done perfectly. And when this was translated to General Mladic, General Mladic laughed very loudly and he held up his right arm like this, and he said, Yes, General Tolimir, he is like my right arm. And then he looked around the room and he saw Colonel Indjic and he took Colonel Indjic's head under his arm here and sort of patted him on the head and said Indjic is likely little toe. So he was appearing to make a contrast between the importance of Indjic and the importance of Tolimir. But it was very clear that he regarded Tolimir as his right arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would have a suggestion to make whether it's down to the speed or something else, we sometimes receive misinterpretation. For instance, in Serbian we heard what the relationship was between General Tolimir and General Smith, and I see that the transcript reads something else. So we kindly ask the Prosecutor and the witness to adopt a slower pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Both very fast speakers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But, in fact, this question by Mr. Elderkin was recorded as we heard it in the original English language. Your observation how was -- Tolimir's relation with General Mladic. Please carry on, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask if you attended any meetings accompanying General Smith in Serbia during July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. I attended a meeting with him at Mrkonjic Grad. I'm sorry, when -- Serbia, yes, of course. I attended a meeting with him in Belgrade which -- or to be specific, I attended Belgrade with him. However, I did not attend the meeting that Smith had with Milosevic in Belgrade. So I went to Belgrade with him as part of his group, but I was not at that meeting. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, I'm just leaving a slightly longer pause.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that meeting in Belgrade was before or after the 19th of July meeting that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure the meeting was before. But I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we now go to Exhibit P740, please. And I'd like to start actually right at the beginning of that video, if we may. It's just a short extract.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll play a short piece of video and afterwards ask you some questions on that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Pause here, please. And that's paused at 1 minute, 19.8 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the two men in that picture starting first with the man wearing the camouflage uniform who has just been working at the printer?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the man who we see just in the centre right of the picture with the moustache?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: This is someone called Milenko Indjic, who was either a major or a lieutenant-colonel - it seemed to fluctuate slightly - who was the person I referred to as the liaison officer based at Lukavica barracks liaising between the Bosnian Serb army and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could continue playing the video a little further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the meeting as we've seen it take place on that -- on that video?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we see, please, Exhibit P603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue with this -- with the next video -- Mr. Elderkin, before you continue with the next video, I would like to ask a question to the witness. Mr. Wood, where was this meeting? Just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, the meeting was held at a restaurant called the Jela restaurant which was close to a village called Han Pijesak, which was the place where the Bosnian Serb army had its headquarters. I never went into Han Pijesak itself, and the restaurant was chosen by Mladic as a meeting-point for this -- which was one of maybe two or three meetings that we had with Mladic out of the glare of publicity, if you like, and slightly private meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall how you got there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We drove there. We -- at the time, we tended to drive in a two-vehicle convoy, usually a Range Rover with Smith, his driver, myself, and Baxter in it. And then a Humvee with a communication team behind and we drove there from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mentioned three persons: Yourself, General Smith and Mr. Baxter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and a driver as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did that mean you were four people in this delegation arriving there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was also the communication team which followed behind. And in the communication team vehicle, usually a woman called Emma Bliss tended to travel as a translator, and if it wasn't her, it was sometimes a man called Tom Dibb, but there was almost always a translator with us who tended to travel in the other vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many people from the Bosnian Serb side attended this meeting which we have seen in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my recollection, there was Mladic, Tolimir, Indjic, plus a collection of drivers, body-guards and so on. So there was perhaps six or seven of them in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall how they got there to this Jela restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well some of them were there when we arrived and had already occupied the restaurant, if you like. On this particular occasion, I think I'm right in saying that Mladic arrived by helicopter, in a Gazelle helicopter, more or less as we arrived. He certainly arrived at one of the meetings in a Gazelle helicopter. On other occasions, he arrived by car, like we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for Exhibit P603 to come up onto the screen, we saw the scene where Generals Smith and Mladic were signing the agreement and making some comments about that. Do you recall where you were in the room while they were sitting up and being filmed up at the top table?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly where I was, but I was -- I mean, there were a number of us in the room out of shot, if you know what I mean, and I think I was one of them. I had printed the agreement as you saw, so I'm pretty certain I was there in the room but not in the camera shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you now look, please, at the document on the screen. Let us know when you have finished looking through the first page. And I'd ask then to move onto the second page.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we see the second page now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, is this the document that you printed out and which was signed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at the point, C, at the top of that second page, the document provides for DutchBat to withdraw on the 21st of July of 1995. Were you present on the occasion of that withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, I was. The -- I had two men -- sorry, two JCOs and an interpreter who were in Srebrenica during the time of the Serb attack and capture of the pocket. And so on the 21st, I went with General Nicolai, who was the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR based at Sarajevo, and we went to -- to -- to witness, if you like, or to help in the evacuation of DutchBat, including my two men from -- from the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you have any opportunity to visit Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. On the way there, we stopped at a restaurant, and I can't remember exactly where it was, and met with General Mladic and his small entourage and had lunch at the restaurant somewhere outside Srebrenica. And after that lunch, Mladic led us down into the village of Srebrenica which, by this time, of course, was occupied entirely by Bosnian Serb forces and which -- and had no civilians in it anymore. And Mladic took us on what I would describe in military terms as a battle-field tour, so a visit around all the key points, if you like, describing what had happened and how the battle had unfolded and essentially telling us how well his men had done. And when that was finished, we then began to move down towards the Dutch battalion camp at Potocari, I think it's called, and as we neared there, Mladic said something like, I have another appointment now, or There is something I must do, or something, and he then left us at the point and that is the last time that I saw him at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And that was all on the 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Apart from this point C at the top of the second page, what -- what was your view at the time of the rest of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Oh, the agreement was a -- was what we would call a paper exercise. At the time, you must remember that Mr. Milosevic, in Belgrade, was giving orders to General Mladic, essentially, and telling him to sign whatever agreements needed to be signed in order to keep UNPROFOR happy at the time. So my interpretation of this agreement signed on the 19th was that it was agreement that neither party attached any importance to and that both parties were signing because it was -- it was just part of a dialogue process, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, please, to the 25th of July. Did you attend any meetings on that date?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And where did you attend a meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Let me just remind myself which meeting this was. Can I just refer to my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It may indeed help if I call up one document on the screen --

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- which is Exhibit P1978, please. And while that's coming up, sir, that's report of the 26th of July from, I think from Colonel Baxter -- Colonel Baxter or Captain Bliss and it describes a meeting on the 25th. So take a moment to look at that and let me know if that helps refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yeah. Yes, this is another meeting at the Jela restaurant. I mentioned that we had two or three. And at the end of this meeting, we moved to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, indeed, if we look at paragraph 2, it describes how after a two-hour meeting, General Smith decided to move to Zepa and resume the meeting with Mladic in order to assess the situation for himself and to initiate with Bosnian agreement the evacuation of the wounded. So as far as you recall, that exactly how the events unfolded?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. We had a similar meeting at the Jela restaurant that I described earlier. And as Baxter has clearly said, we then moved from there, all of us together, to a point in the woods just above the village of Zepa where the meeting then continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you describe that location, as far as you recall. How did it look? What, if any, facilities were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- the village of Zepa is in the bottom of a very steep valley, wooded valley. And the road that ran down to it from the direction that we arrived was a zigzag road that ran down through the woods, and at the top of that slope, so we're talking about, you know, a kilometre or two away from Zepa and quite a lot higher, in some woods there, was a flat area in which there was some tents drawn up, some vehicles parked, and that was where we had the meeting -- or, that was where Smith had the continuation of the meeting with Mladic in order to -- in order, as he says, to co-ordinate, if you like, the evacuation of wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How did you and General Smith and his entourage travel to that location?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: By vehicle again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know how General Mladic travelled there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, and I mentioned before that he had arrived and departed in a helicopter on a previous -- or, on one of the meetings. It is possible that this is the meeting that he arrived and departed by helicopter; but, if not, then he drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And who was present up at this -- this higher location above the town?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Mladic was there, Tolimir was there, Indjic was there. Obviously from our side, Smith, Baxter, myself. I believe Tom Dibb was there; I can't recall him there, but I believe he was there. And I believe Emma Bliss may have been there. And then there were quite a collection of other Bosnian Serb officers and soldiers that were there as part of force that had captured the village of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like to refer briefly to your statement and understand whether when you say Tolimir was present at this hilltop location, if that's actually your recollection, or whether you saw Tolimir at another location in the vicinity that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I saw Tolimir -- I mean, remember that I was at that location at the top of the hill for quite some time. Later on, I went down into the village of Zepa where, again, Tolimir was, but he certainly had been at the top of the hill at other points in the day, because I -- I've been shown a video that shows him, I think, at the top of a hill at some point on one of those days. But that is not to say that he was not in the village of Zepa later on when I went down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And apart from the UNPROFOR members and the Bosnian Serb army who you saw at the location at the top of the hill, did you see any Bosnian Muslims at that location on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: There was one man who was -- I would describe him as being late 30s, early 40s, tall, dark hair, wearing a pale-coloured shirt who was described as being the mayor or some sort of local head of the community down in Zepa. And he was there at some point in the meeting in order to -- in order to make some agreement with Mladic, effectively, at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: From what you observed, how was he behaving?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: He looked shaken and frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity, yourself, to communicate with him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Not that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you've mentioned already that you, at some point, were down in the Zepa village. How did you travel down to the village?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: At some point in the time spent at the top of the hill, I was asked to go down into the village, I think to find some more people to come up to be part of the meeting, but I'm not certain about that. But I drove down with Major Indjic and with the -- and with one of the Serb officers, drove down in one of the vehicles, and drove down this zigzag hill into the village of Zepa that was maybe a kilometre or two away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about this other Serb officer?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Court what you saw as you travelled down from the hilltop location towards the village.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: The first thing that I recall is that at the top of the hill, having left the clearing area that I described and gone onto the track that led down into Zepa, at the top of the hill, parked on the left, was a captured British manufactured Saxon armoured personnel carrier, which had been obviously captured by the Bosnian Serbs at some point and had been re-sprayed green and black in camouflage, because, of course, previously it would have been white, that was parked up at the top of the hill with a collection of Bosnian Serb soldiers standing around it. We then drove down into the village of Zepa, and as we came into the village, we drove through various orchards and little fields that surrounded the village and in those fields I could see small groups of Bosnian Serb soldiers who were doing what I would call regrouping after an action. So they were collecting themselves together, they were refilling magazines, they were cleaning weapons, they were generally sorting themselves out after having been busy. And we drove on down into the village itself where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you go on to describe the scene when you arrived in the village.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, the village of Zepa is a very small village, very primitive. My recollection is that it consisted entirely of wooden huts, wooden houses. I remember a water wheel at one point that was turning and, presumably, milling grain or something. And in the middle of the village was a slightly clear area, not really a village square, but a slightly clear area, in which there were a number of buses drawn up. I remember maybe four or five buses drawn up, and what appeared to be quite a large number of mainly women and children, but also some old people, men and women, who were being organised in the square prior to being loaded onto these buses and evacuated. And these obviously were the occupants of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who was doing the organising; did you see?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. In the square was a group of about seven or eight Bosnian Serb policemen and they were being directed by General Tolimir. And General Tolimir, who I recognised, obviously very clearly, from having met him on previous occasions, was walking around, directing the movement of these women and children and directing the activities of the policemen loading the women and children into the coaches. And he had his pistol out, sort of held up like this, and was -- was -- I saw no violence being visited on the people, but it was a very threatening atmosphere. And the people there, you know, were clearly very frightened and distresses, and it was being directed, as I say, by General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: For the record, sir, when you said that General Tolimir had his pistol held like this, you had raised your right arm, bent upwards with the forearm pointing towards the ceiling. And so the Serb policemen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you state that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should explain, sorry. He was -- I remember very clearly General Tolimir. I remember what he was wearing. I remember him walking around, and he had as -- as I have been -- as I have been reminded, he had his right hand -- held his pistol in his right hand. He had it pointing up at the sky. He wasn't pointing it at anybody. He wasn't overtly threatening people with it, but he had it in his hand and it was held, you know, pointing up at the sky at about shoulder height. And the whole -- the whole episode was a little bit like -- was a little bit like being in a 1940s newsreel. There was a sort of sense -- there was a sense of the Holocaust about it. If it had been black and white, it would have been more -- you know, it would have been more in keeping in sense with the scene that was unfolding around me. And it was a very strange experience for me to be standing there as an UN soldier in a blue beret standing there amongst what was very obviously an unpleasant act of, admittedly non-violent at that stage, ethnic cleansing that was going on, directed by General Tolimir and his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How were the Serb policemen dressed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. But I suspect -- I remember them as Serb policemen and the Serb policemen at the time used to wear a sort of blue and black camouflage uniform. So my assumption is that's what they were wearing, but I don't remember clearly what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, I don't clearly remember that they were armed, but I'm almost certain they must have been armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned you recall how General Tolimir was dressed. Could you describe that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing -- he was wearing the normal green camouflage clothing that you have seen photographs of. He was also wearing a sort of sleeveless green top on top of that, and he was wearing his little peaked Serb officer's cap with the short stubby peak on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we go back again, please, to Exhibit P740 and this time just play a short clip from 20 minutes and 26 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: This is taken from a video shot on 26th of July, so I'd simply concentrate on the image rather than on the surrounding events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you recognise any of the individuals we've just seen in that footage?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Obviously I recognise Mladic and Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And having seen how Tolimir was dressed in this footage, does that correspond with how you recall he looked on the day you saw him in Zepa town?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. He -- he wasn't -- on the video, he wasn't wearing the sort of little jacket on top, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we perhaps go back a bit in the video and stop at a certain point in time that you really can identify the persons shown in this video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, I am mistaken. He is wearing the jacket. There we are. I didn't see it in the first instance when he came past. That is Tolimir in the centre of it, wearing the cap that I described, wearing the clothes I described, and wearing the little jacket that I mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And for the record, the video is paused at 20 minutes, 36.8 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. Regarding this picture, you've given us a description of General Tolimir, because, see, there is a belt, and I see something near his belt. Could you tell us what we can see there? Is this -- what is this? Is it a pouch for grenades? Or what can we see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, looking at it, that that is the pouch that I mentioned to you earlier on, that -- in which he kept a small grenade. Perhaps if we advance the video a frame or two, it would make it a clearer picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honours, I think the clearest shot is right at the beginning of the clip that we just played. So it would help to go back to 20 minutes, 26 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes. You can see that is a little pouch, and that is the pouch that he showed me when we met at Pale in April that had a little round grenade in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Page 22 of today's transcript, lines 2 to 4, you were describing General Tolimir. You say: "He had his right hand -- he held his pistol in his right hand pointing up to the sky."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: In the circumstances in which you were, how else should he have held his gun? Can you explain that to me as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a soldier, myself, at the time, if I was supervising people, women and children to get on a coach, I wouldn't have had my gun out at all. I'm not sure why he had it out, because he wasn't -- certainly, when I saw him, he wasn't actually pointing it at people to threaten them to do things. He was just waving it around as a sort of a -- like a status symbol, like a sort of power symbol, if you like. It's not something I would have done, but that is -- that is what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, just to follow up from Judge Nyambe's question, if a soldier or officer has a handgun, where can they put it, apart from having it in their hand?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, most soldiers would have a holster. Most of them would be on the belt, some might have a shoulder holster. And most of the time, generally speaking, the rule is, that unless you want to use the pistol, you leave it in the holster. You only take it out if you want to threaten somebody with it, or shoot somebody with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you carrying any weapons on the 25th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, I had a pistol too, and it was in my holster.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, did General Smith travel down to Zepa village on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No, he didn't. As far as I recall, I was the only person of our party who went down into Zepa that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How long did you spend down in Zepa that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Probably no more than 20 minutes, half an hour or so. And I don't really remember whether we achieved whatever it was we were sent to do. I don't remember bringing somebody up from the village. I think that -- I think that when we got there, it was clear that there weren't any other men that we could take up to be part of whatever was going on at the top. So after 20 or 30 minutes, we simply drove back up the hill and rejoined the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt for a moment. I just want to know, we have this video and the still on the screen at the moment. Were you present during this situation when General Mladic, General Tolimir were there? What is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This video, I believe, is taken on the 26th. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. At the moment it's a question for you. Do --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have seen the video --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: -- can you recall the situation which is depicted in this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't believe that I was there on the 26th. I'm not certain I was not there, but I don't believe I was there. I was there on the 25th and there on the 27th, and I may have been there on the 26th, but I have no clear recollection of it, and I don't recall being at the meeting that is depicted in the video. I think that was an entirely Serb meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just to stay a moment longer with your time in the Zepa village, what was the atmosphere while you were down there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, and at the risk of sounding too dramatic about it, it was little bit like standing in a scene from the Holocaust, in the sense that there were maybe 300, 400 women and children, around about that number, and some old people, all of whom seemed obviously very distressed, very frightened, a lot of children, and were all being herded onto the buses prior to being taken away. The atmosphere, therefore, was one of -- was one of fear, threatening, no actual violence, but certainly the threat of violence. And, for me, it was very uncomfortable because it was -- you know, it was clearly a very -- a very significant event and standing there as a -- as the only member of UNPROFOR in amongst it, and really unable to intervene and not in a position to intervene, it was a very strange position to be in. And I remember talking to Indjic, who stood beside me, and asking him very pointedly whether he had children, because many of the people were children, so there were lots of mothers with babies and with toddlers, and so on. And Indjic said to me, Yes, I have a daughter of 13 and a son of 7, or something like. And I said to him, you know, So how do you feel? And he didn't say anything. He didn't reply. I don't know what he felt, but I felt that he ought to be ashamed of this sort of conduct being done, you know, in his name by his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you speak to General Tolimir at any point during your time in Zepa village?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: At the time in the village itself, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I just wonder if you can amplify on your statement at page 27, lines 19 to 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'll read it out for you. You state: "As the only member of UNPROFOR in amongst it, and really unable to intervene and not in a position to intervene, it was a very strange position to be in." As a member of UNPROFOR, if you had intervened what would you have done? Or what should you have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a good question to which there isn't a very good answer. Had there been actual violence, in other words, if I had actually seen one of the policemen beating or threatening or shooting one of the non-combatants there, then I would have certainly intervened to prevent that or tried to prevent that from happening. As I said before, I didn't see that. There wasn't any actual violence that I saw while I was is there, and, therefore, there was no practical intervention I could have taken, really. In a sense, I felt that being there was probably acting as a slight deterrent from actual violence being visited upon these people by the Serb forces. But, nevertheless, there was, as I described, this palpable sense of fear, threat, disruption, if you like. And as to what I could have done about that, the answer is nothing much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question. You said: "... then I would have certainly intervened ..." In a case, if you have observed any direct violence, what do you mean by "intervened"? What means did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not very much, I accept. And we're talking here hypothetically, obviously, because it didn't happen. But I would like to think that, as a British Army officer and as a member of UNPROFOR, if I had seen, let us say, one of the Serb policemen beating up one of the women or children or taking her away, you know, for something, then I would like to think that I would have at least been able to verbally remonstrate. And if the worst came to the worst, been able to use force, although I was by myself, to prevent that from happening. Remember, UNPROFOR was authorised to use force only in self-defence, essentially, and remember that I only had a pistol with me, so there is a limit to what I could have done. But my experience in these matters was that, generally speaking, if one confronted people with the magnitude of what they were doing, they sometime would back down and stop, so although this didn't happen, I do stress this didn't happen, I think that had there been violence there, I might have been able to prevent some of it by simply being there and by simply witnessing it and remonstrating, if you like, with the people who were doing it. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you see very well that this portion of your testimony is extremely important for the Chamber and it's quite troublesome for me as well. I'm wondering if we're talking about the same reality. On page 27 of the transcript, you say - I'm going to try to translated from French to English myself, or English to French, rather -- you're saying that this situation seemed like a scene from the Holocaust. We all know what that means, of course. But then, at the same time, in answering a question put by Judge Nyambe, you say that you could not intervene directly because there was no direct violence. And you are giving an example, a situation in which a member of the UNPROFOR would have been violated upon. So I would like to know, could you have reacted against a very small amount of violence against a member of your mission, of the UNPROFOR, or could you have not done anything with respect to something that you, yourself, called the Holocaust? So if I understood correctly, this is quite a dramatic situation. I mean, I don't know if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand the question you're asking me, but I can re-stress the fact that this was, as you say, quite a dramatic situation. There are relatively few points in one's live, certainly in my life, when you find yourself at the point of history, if you like. You see something happening around you that you know is highly significant whether you're part of it or not. And this is one of the occasions in my life where I have felt very strongly that I was at the point of history. I was witnessing with my own eyes activity that was historic in the sense that it was something that people would pour over in the future and be brought to account for in the future, which is one of the reasons why I recollect it so clearly, because amongst all the episodes I witnessed in Bosnia, it was one of the most significant. But I don't -- I may not have answered your question clearly because I'm not quite sure what you were asking me in your question. Perhaps you could rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I will not rephrase my question. I will not put my question again. Maybe I'll just make a comment here. You're talking about a very dramatic situation and you say that this situation will be part of history. At the same time, you, yourself, recognised your incapacity of reacting because there was not a sufficient amount of violence against somebody from your mission, for instance. This is what astonished me. This is why I am surprised. I'm quite happy with your answer, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You want to comment on that, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, thank you. The only comment I would make, if it helps, is that part of the problem with UNPROFOR was that it was insufficiently resourced and insufficiently mandated to do many of the things that one might have wished to have done in the whole episode of the Balkan wars. What we're looking at here is one tiny episode that really encapsulates that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. Just following up on my earlier question and on Judge Mindua's comments, and I may not refer to a particular page of the transcript, and if I recollect wrongly, please do not hesitate to intervene. You have given evidence today which suggests that you met General Tolimir on a number of occasions. You had lunch, meetings that were quite -- not as dramatic as the scene you are explaining now. You have told us about how he talked to you about the pouch with the hand grenade, and what have you. Here, you are standing at the point of history, a situation which you are describing is ethnic cleansing directed by General Tolimir with his gun. Don't you -- is it possible for you to have then have intervened by, saying, asking General Tolimir, not to hold his gun in the way he held it because you perceived it as something that was frightening the population around you. Is that something that you could have done? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the benefit of hindsight, perhaps it is. But we're overlooking the fact that General Tolimir knew very well what he was doing. He was holding his gun that way in order to frighten the population. So me asking him not to do it would not have necessarily been helpful. It might have helped my conscience, but it wouldn't have helped the situation necessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you go back to Zepa after the 25th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned before, I certainly went back on the 27th. I may have gone back on the 26th, but I don't recall clearly. But after those two days, I don't believe I went back at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, finally, do you recall attending a meeting on the 31st of July of 1995 at Mrkonjic Grad?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could see, please, Exhibit P594.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, again, this is a video, to start, please, at 1 hour, 2 minutes, and 39 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the video played.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: We were just calling it up, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And just pause the video at 1 hour, 2 minutes, 59.3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us if you recognise anyone in the shot now?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. In that room, you can see standing -- you can see Colonel Baxter. Sitting half turned from us is Emma Bliss. Sitting facing the camera, but half hidden, is myself. And I think the blurred figure sitting down is General Smith. Go you rewind a frame or two, I will be able to confirm that. Yes, that is it General Smith then sitting between Emma Bliss and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we have just gone back to 1 hour, 2 minutes 58.3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that this video has already been admitted as P594. What was not admitted at the time of the video's admission was the accompanying transcript. I would propose that be admitted simply to make sense of what's already effectively contained within the video, and that's 65 ter 1757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what was the reason why we just MFI'd this document. Perhaps we didn't have a transcript at that time. Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I believe the transcript was simply overlooked at the time. As for the reason this was MFI'd, I understand that because it's a compilation video we're intending to present other witnesses to cover the range of material. Sorry. I understand that the exhibit itself isn't MFI'd at all. So I'm referring to a different compilation. This one, the video is admitted. The transcript itself was overlooked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were giving us the 65 ter number as 1757 related to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that's uploaded and it should be part of the video so that we have only one P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this transcript will be part of P594.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I don't have any further questions at this time for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, now Mr. Tolimir has the opportunity and the right to put questions to you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone. May there be peace in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not mine. We will follow up from what the witness has just been telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You presented here this view of yours, your vision that it was Tolimir who was walking across the village wielding a pistol. Do you have any eye-witness who would be able to confirm this? We've had a number of witnesses appearing here, none of whom mentioned this detail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: If you mean eye-witnesses who are not members of the Bosnian Serb army or, indeed, part of the Muslim population, then, as I said before, I was the only member of UNPROFOR who was down in that village at that time, as I recollect. So apart from myself, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it Mr. Edward Joseph and Mr. Bezruchenko, as well as the president of the War Presidency of Zepa, Muharem Hajric, and Avdo Palic who boarded the civilians onto buses, or was the Army of Republika Srpska that was doing this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I have no idea on whose authority it was being done. I saw the actual boarding being done by the policemen I described earlier and you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show D173. This is a report by a witness appearing here before you, Mr. Edward Joseph, and we will be quoting from his statement as to what it was he had to say about the evacuation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You see the statement there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to page 3, please. This is Mr. Joseph's statement. Let's look at paragraph 14 on page 3 which reads: "Evacuation started the same morning when several Serb-owned buses and trucks arrived to the centre. We started to organise the civilians boarding in the vehicles ... Viktor, and at least one French officer -- I, Viktor, and at least one French officer were very active on this as well as some of the Muslim civilian leaders. Can I recall seeing also General Smith there, observing the evacuation. "I remember a group of wounded ABiH soldiers being among the evacuees. Soon after the evacuations started, a medical examination was conducted for them ... by a French and Serb ... doctor," et cetera. Can you tell Their Honours, are you at all acquainted with Edward Joseph and Viktor Bezruchenko? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't remember either of them. You might have to remind me about who Edward Joseph is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't remember, there is no need for me to remind you. Well, he was a civilian representative of UNPROFOR. Since you're not familiar with them, did you see any UNPROFOR representatives in Zepa at a time -- at the time that you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I've already stated that I did not. In Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you give us the time and date of your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, the date you already have. The time, I would be estimating --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please state it for the transcript, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Let me just refer to my statement so I make sure I get it correct. It was the 25th of July. In terms of the time, I would only be estimating; but, given that we had -- well, in fact, in my statement, I say later in the afternoon. So it would simply be an estimate, but I would say between 3.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, could you tell us at which papers are you looking at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm looking at my own statement given -- I don't know -- has a reference number on it. But the statement I gave in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement was given on the 14th of April, 2008, and given in London. And I believe I'm looking at a version of the statement which I believe has been provided to the -- to the accused. And on page 2 of that, paragraph 5, I describe the meeting in the Jela restaurant and then the movement to Zepa. And I say about four lines down: "Later that afternoon, while Smith and Mladic met at the table on the top of the hill above Zepa, I went down into the village ..." So my estimate is that it would be sometime mid-afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This statement was given to representatives of the OTP, of the Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand so. I understand that -- I forget what the term is, but a version was given to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It would help to clarify, Your Honours, the statement is an OTP witness statement provided during an interview by members of the OTP with Lieutenant-Colonel Wood, and following the UK's Rule 70 clearance of redacted version of the statement, it's been disclosed to the Defence. And I believe it appears on their list of potential exhibits as 1D613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. David, you shouldn't mind me asking for the exact time and date. Since this was registered by UNPROFOR and VRS, we know exactly where Tolimir was, whether he was in Zepa, accompanying the first convoy or the second. You shouldn't mind me asking for that. After all, I am defending myself in a court of law. Let's see what Joseph has to say about the weapons and this scene which gives you a sense of Holocaust. At page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir repeat the transcript page of Mr. Joseph's testimony. It was too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment we don't receive interpretation. Please repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's transcript page 10601, lines 6 through 7, where Mr. Joseph said: "But, General Tolimir, you were in down-town Zepa. I do not recall whether you, yourself, carried any weapons." My learned friend Mr. Elderkin can have his say now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It's only fair if General Tolimir is going to refer to Mr. Joseph's evidence to state the date on which he is talking about, and that's the 26th of July. The witness has confirmed that he was in Zepa on the 25th of July, the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said that Edward Joseph testified on the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: If he doesn't recall me carrying any weapons, how do you reconcile the fact that you remember me wielding a gun, so -- and that it was so firmly impressed in your memory that it reminded you of Holocaust?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I think that it's been established we're talking about two different occasions here. And on the occasion that I saw you with your gun in your hand, there was no one else of Mr. Joseph's description in Zepa with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you weren't accompanied by anyone. You saw what he said in his statement, that he drew up lists in the morning. Let's look at paragraph 16 and 17 of the statement you have on your screen. I'm quoting from paragraph 16, and this is what Edward Joseph said: "We created written lists of the evacuees, and, as far as I can recall, we had a separate list for each vehicle. I turned over those lists at a later date, either to UNHCR or someone in UNPROFOR. We tried to place one UNPROFOR soldier on each vehicle, but I'm not sure if we managed to do it throughout the time. "The evacuation lasted probably three days or longer. The atmosphere was very tense throughout the time but we managed to board all the people who had come to the centre and were willing to leave. I estimate that approximately 7.000 people were evacuated." This is my question: If Mr. Joseph, who was involved in the evacuation and the drawing up of lists said, and I'm quoting only the relevant portion, "We boarded all the people who had come to the centre and were willing to leave," does this mean that the Army of Republika Srpska did not engage in any sort of triage, screening, or separation of individuals but, rather, that it was done solely by the individuals I referred to earlier on: Mr. Bezruchenko, Hajric, Avdo Palic, and they had a say in who was to leave or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I have no idea what process was used to organise the people who were evacuated from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we must have our first break now, on technical reasons. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. David -- sorry, Mr. Wood, we have been discussing the beginning of the evacuation for which you said happened on the 25th. You said you arrived at 3.00. My question is whether the evacuation began when you arrived or has -- had it already been under way?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: You remember that I estimated it was around 3.00. No, the evacuation appeared to have -- to be under way already. But I hadn't seen any evacuation prior to that, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why, in your view -- or why do you believe there were only members of the VRS in Zepa and not those mentioned by Mr. Joseph in his statement, who organised the evacuation itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You could see in his statement that he said he evacuated all those who arrived in the centre, so no one was left. Do you know from any source whether anyone was singled out, taken off the buses and returned during the process of the evacuation you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, going back to Edward Joseph's statement, I think it has been established that his statement concerns the following day, not the day I was there. In answer to your question about whether I know of anyone taken off the buses, the answer to that is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. General Joseph's -- sorry, Mr. Joseph's statement was given before the testimony and it concerns the entire evacuation. I quoted a particular part in which he says he cannot recall whether I had any weapons on me. It wasn't actually his statement but a single sentence that I pointed out. Actually, it was from his testimony on the 10th, I believe. This is but a small excerpt. I think he uttered it on March 1 at transcript page 10601. Did you know that the War Presidency, itself, and Avdo Palic, as well as UNPROFOR representatives, organised the evacuation process from Zepa and that it wasn't done by the VRS. It wasn't the VRS soldiers who carried out any screening or who decided who was to board the buses or not. Were you able to observe that in the centre of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I've already told you what I saw in the centre of Zepa, which was you organising a group of, what I took to be, Bosnian Serb policemen, organising the loading onto vehicles of a few hundred women and children, mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that I was wielding out a gun, thus carrying out ethnic cleansing. I'm asking you, as a soldier, does a general secure the soldiers in his environment or that are a part of his escort; or are they there to secure, to provide security for the general? Does General Smith take out his handgun when you are a part of his escort?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't think there's much doubt that there's a big difference between the sort of general that General Smith is and the sort of general that you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But this doesn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The point I'm taking -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the real response to the question of Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would not normally expect a normal general to be wielding his pistol in these circumstances. That's really my point. Why General Tolimir was wielding his pistol at that -- on that occasion is something we can only speculate about. But -- but the question he asked is: Is this something a general would normally do, and the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, the question was slightly different: "Does General Smith take out his handgun when you are a part of his escort?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No was the answer. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Wood. Let us look at D51, which is agreement of the 24th of July. We'll look into how it came about that the population was evacuated. We'll see the agreement itself. It is on the screens now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is the agreement on the disarmament of the able-bodied population in the Zepa enclave, signed by the Rogatica Brigade commander, Rajko Kusic; Dudnjik Semjon, who was there as the UNPROFOR commander for Zepa; as well as Ratko Mladic and Hamdija Torlak. It was signed on 24th of July, 1995; that is to say, one day prior to your arrival. Let's look at item 1. It says: "A cease-fire between the parties to the conflict shall be implemented immediately." My question is this: If there's cease-fire, why use weapons? Of what use are weapons in that situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite sure how to answer that question. If there was a cease-fire, then I would not expect weapons to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be logical for General Tolimir to take out his weapon surrounded by inhabitants of the area who were departing, who were actually civilian? Does it make any sense?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, as I said earlier, I can only speculate as to why you had your pistol out. But it makes sense if the purpose was to frighten the population. Otherwise, it makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why would I try to scare them if they were to leave for the territory where I lived and worked and they were supposed to traverse many kilometres? Why would I try to scare them by pulling out a handgun? Can you explain that to the Chamber perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, again, you're asking me to explain your actions and I'm unable to do that. I can speculate that, for whatever reason, you wanted to continue the atmosphere of fear and intimidation that was evident in Zepa that afternoon, but I cannot explain your actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the inhabitants start running away when they saw me wielding the handgun and did they give up on being evacuated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No. The inhabitants that I saw were thoroughly frightened, very frightened, and many of them, as I mentioned, were either old or infirm or they were mothers with children. So I didn't see any run away. But I would question whether any of them could have run away, even if they'd wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, you told the Chamber that you saw me wielding a handgun, pointing upwards, conducting ethnic cleansing. Let's look at item 3 of the agreement, and there you can see perhaps whether I ordered the ethnic cleansing to be carried out or was this a provision of the agreement, mutually agreed to by both sides, and I merely took part in it. Paragraph 3: "The civilian and able-bodied population of Zepa shall assemble around the UNPROFOR base in Zepa, which will be a sign to the Army of the RS that the units under the command of Avdo Palic have accepted the truce and will not try to take advantage of it." My question is: Were the VRS and its officers in any way outnumbered or in an inferior position, vis-a-vis the local population, so as to feel they had to defend themselves in this way?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No. As I've already testified, there were probably 3- or 400 people, local inhabitants there, and there were, in my estimate, about 8 or 9 -- 7, 8, or 9 policemen and yourself there so they were not outnumbered -- so they were outnumbered, I beg your pardon. But they were outnumbered by women and children and old people. There was not, in my opinion, a reason to -- to use military force, by which I would mean the brandishing of weapons or the using of weapons, in order to achieve the objective that you appeared to be trying to achieve, which was loading them onto the coaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would such conduct divert people's attention away from the process of evacuation or would they help evacuation in any way?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: When you say "such action," you mean waving guns around?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Precisely. Would brandishing a weapon by any Serb officer further persuade those Muslims to leave, or would it divert their attention or put them in a position which they would decide not to proceed with the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, as I've previously said, I can only speculate as to why you had your weapon out. But my speculation is that you may have wanted to do so, in order to further frighten the people who were already quite frightened so as to encourage them to conform with your instructions and to get into the buses and leave quietly. But that is purely my interpretation of what it is you were doing. I don't know what your purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to a footage to see how it all began and whether they were, indeed, afraid of my gun, which, by the way, I did not even have, let's look at item 7 [Realtime transcript read in error "3"]: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949, and the Additional Protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." My question is this: Since they were provided freedom of movement during the hostilities, is it ethnic cleansing, indeed, because the agreement is quite clear on the issue of evacuation only while hostilities continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just for the record, it seems that General Tolimir is quoting from item 7, rather than item 3 as it appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Indeed. Now the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
