utterances.text: I am not quite sure how I can answer this question. The -- I don't have a definition of what "ethnic cleansing" is or means. It is clear to me -- it was clear to me, standing in the square in Zepa, that those who were being loaded onto the buses were being evacuated from Zepa against their will. If that is what is defined by "ethnic cleansing," then that's what was occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you whether you said that General Tolimir ordered for the ethnic cleansing to take place. I believe that was your formulation. But telling us that I took out a gun and brandished it, did you try to present the situation as a situation of Holocaust in order to give a certain impression for the Court, or did you have any other motives for that, any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, you've asked two questions there. As to the first one, whether you ordered it or not, I do not know that. I've only testified that you were directing it. I can only speculate as to whether you ordered it, and I'm making a distinction between the physical carrying out of the action on the ground which I saw you do and the orders for it, which I did not see, and I cannot comment on who gave. With regards to the second question, what I have tried to do for clarity is to explain the sense that I got, as I stood in the square in Zepa and saw the actions of you and your men, and I have equated it to visions of the Holocaust simply to convey the sense of fear, the sense of oppression that I witnessed. As I've stressed already, I did not see any direct -- any direct acts of violence, but what I did see was the use of military force, fear, and coercion to evacuate a civilian population which, at that point, consisted almost entirely of women, children, and old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at P5704. It is a footage taken in Zepa on the 25th of July. Let's have a look at it at 36 minutes, 15 seconds, to 37 minutes, 50 seconds. Actually, the exhibit is P740.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see a person in uniform in the centre of the screen. Do you know who it is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Do you mean in the near ground? Close to the camera?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a single person in uniform in this still. At this moment, his back is turned to us, but when we play it again, we'll see the face. But, in any case, do you already know who that person is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't believe I do. If you rewind it a couple of frames, I'll have another look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We did rewind. Do you know Avdo Palic, commander of the Zepa Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this person part of the VRS in the way he is moving about, or do you believe that he is freely moving about -- moving among the population as part of that population?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Are you talking about the person on the screen now? This person? Perhaps you could rewind the video so that I can see what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we need always for the record the time when the video was stopped. I think this is at 37 minutes, .6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should rewind a bit more, as requested by the witness, so that he could see whether this particular person is escorting anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see him move.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see the person holding the papers in his hand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see the person with some papers in his hand?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I saw him. If you could rewind again, I can get a better picture of him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You saw it well, I believe. You saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- a number of sheets of paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, we stopped at 37.21 minutes. We saw two people with paper in their hands. Are you referring to this person on the right-hand side of the screen in the blue shirt?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, that is the person. And there was another person whom I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who the person in the blue shirt is with the stack of paper in his hand?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know the president of the War Presidency of Zepa, Mr. Mehmed Hajric?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. From the documents sent by UNPROFOR representatives from Zepa, did you ever learn that he and the other person who we could see created those lists and that they were in charge of evacuation, deciding who was to board what bus at what time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, that is what your document appears to say, but you're showing me a video of a different event from the event that I described to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will ascertain whether this footage was taken on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will go on playing the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Am I holding a handgun or shaking hands with the gentleman who was the Zepa Brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: You're shaking his hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The video was stopped at 37.45 -- 49 minutes. You should indicate that, Mr. Tolimir. It's not my duty. It's your examination. But we need to have it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I've just only realised where it was that you were reading it from. I can see it now clearly on the screen, 37.49. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see three individuals here, one of whom is me? Do you recognise the other two?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't recognise them, but you have told me that the man shaking your hand was the ex-commander of the Zepa Brigade. But I don't refreshing either of the other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a good look at the other individual because you'll see him in another frame as a negotiator. I can't remember his name now. Don't you see here that I'm in contact with representatives of Zepa who signed the agreement on evacuation? Since this is one of the negotiators and the other person being the brigade commander, does it not transpire that they agreed to the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, I cannot possibly comment on what they may or may not have agreed with, with you. What you have shown me is a video-clip of you appearing to greet or maybe say good-bye to a man on the right who you tell me is the ex-brigade commander. I have no idea what passed between you, either before or after that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That wasn't my question. I wanted to tell you this: Do they in any way exhibit fear? We have the other individual smiling. So did they react with fear when they saw me? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, I must emphasise, I was not present when this video was taken, so I can't comment on whether they were frightened or not. In this particular frame, they don't look particularly frightened, I will agree. But, then, again, they knew they were being video'd I cannot make a comment as to whether they were actually frightened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the beginning of the evacuation on the 25th. And this is there for the Trial Chamber to ascertain. The footage was provided by the Prosecution, not by me. Can we play it -- oh no, that's the extent of the footage. Let's read something to see how the evacuation came about. Can we have P740. It's the same footage but we'll be reviewing the portion from 25 to 26 minutes, and if the audio is too poor, I'll read out later on what was said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we stop there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago, in the frame showing the centre of Zepa, was it this individual that you saw there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the video was stopped at 25.19. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks like the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now continue playing the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please pay attention to what you can hear and read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When General Mladic asked, What do you want? The person in the white shirt said, He doesn't know. I'll speak. And that's Hamdija Torlak, the signatory to the agreement I showed you a moment ago, pursuant to which the evacuation took place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue playing the video, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop, please. We need the time when you stopped the video. Every time you stop the video you should indicate, like all parties have to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The video was stopped at 25 minutes, 49 seconds. Can we continue playing it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear the representative or the signatory to the agreement say, We called our government. Were you able to hear this, or read this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I didn't see that, no. Perhaps you could rewind it till --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say this was at 26 minutes, 8 seconds when we stopped the footage. And the witness wants it rewound in order for him to see and hear what Mr. Torlak said. So can we rewind, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Rather than waste time by reviewing this footage which the Trial Chamber has had occasion to look at repeatedly, I would like to draw your attention to some of the interesting parts of the transcript. We've stopped the clip at 27 minutes, 3 seconds. And I'll tell you what transpired in these several minutes, since the audio was quite poor, at least from what I was able to hear. The transcript says: "We called our government," et cetera, "now we've come here to try and arrange one thing. We agreed that under the circumstances, the issue of Zepa is best resolved by having the entire population of Zepa leave safely and of free will." That's what Hamdija Torlak said, who signed the agreement and asked for the evacuation of the people. He was the president of the local government and, at the same time, the president of the War Presidency of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should call up the transcript. In the subtitles we have seen, there was a different language. There was -- I didn't see anything about that these people have called their government. I didn't see that. And if you are reading from text, you should call -- call it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have a transcript of the video which I was reading from. And as for the video footage itself, I don't know -- I don't speak English. He said, We called the government. He didn't say, We called the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we need the document on the screen, the transcript. I don't have it. We have to check it. And if you want to put a question to this part of the transcript to the witness, he should see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 13 of the transcript? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is the document number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 740. Thank you. That's from 25 minutes to 26 minutes. That's the portion of the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This can't be the relevant part of the transcript, at least in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In both languages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As we can see, line 27, in Serbian, that's where I'm reading from. In English, that's line 2 or 3. It reads: "Hamdija Torlak says [unintelligible]," so the person transcribing couldn't make it out. "In our work," et cetera, "we came to try to arrange one thing. We agreed that in this situation the issue of Zepa would be resolved in the best way if the entire population left the zone of Zepa safely." That's the line that I wanted to read out and that was the foundation for the question I was going to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still don't see any reference to the government or any of the quote that General Tolimir previously read out, and I think it would help, since he spent some time narrating that, to identify where that is, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that was my concern as well. Page 55, lines 5 through 9, Mr. Tolimir, you told the Chamber the transcript says and then you quoted: "We called our government," et cetera, "now we have come here to try and arrange one thing. We agreed that under the circumstances, the issue of Zepa is best resolved, by having the entire population of Zepa leave safely and of free will." I don't see this text here in the document in front of us. It is it quite similar, but without this mentioning of any government. Could you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see where it reads "unintelligible" as written by someone who, for the purposes of the Prosecution, transcribed this. And then it goes on to say, "In our work," et cetera. However, in Serbian, we can hear the person say, "We called our government," et cetera, and then from there continues the text. "We came here to try to arrange one thing. We agreed that in this situation the issue of Zepa would best be resolved if the entire population left the zone of Zepa safely." I don't know what the English reads because I can't speak English. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's still a difference. We can't make it out. You should put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So based on what you see here, who asked that the civilian population be evacuated, a representative of the VRS or a representative of the civilian population, here in the person of Hamdija Torlak, in the process of negotiating with General Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, it appears from the transcript that you've offered and the video that you've offered that that -- that the person who you've identified as the lead Bosnian Muslim says, We come here to try to arrange one thing. So the implication is that they are seeking to arrange something. But you're asking me to comment on -- on a dialogue that I was not present at, that I have no knowledge of, and so I can't really tell you what was meant by either party in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I put this to you because you said that I had ordered ethnic cleansing, whereas, it's the president of the executive committee of the municipal assembly doing that. Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I object to the question because the witness was very clear about saying he had no knowledge of who ordered the ethnic cleansing. He simply saw General Tolimir directing the process down in Zepa town and it appears to be a deliberate misstatement of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can go back to the transcript of today. Page 22, lines 10 to 14, and I quote: "It was a very strange experience for me to be standing there as a UN soldier in a blue beret, standing there amongst what was very obviously an unpleasant act of admittedly non-violent ethnic cleansing going on directed by General Tolimir and his men." This was -- the witness who has testified about this situation this morning, this is the basic -- we are now discussing on and Mr. Tolimir is putting questions in relation to that. We should be very precise in choosing our words. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I don't have the direct reference but I clearly recall an answer where the witness distinguished, in his view, military terms between ordering and directing. I think that should be reflected, if the question is put back to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, he was asked later in relation to this first answer. The first answer included the words "directed by General Tolimir and his men." "Directed," I repeat. So later on there was a more precise explanation. I don't know where it is in the transcript, but you should continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember a frame from the video featuring an individual whose name appeared on the screen as Hamdija -- or, rather, Mehmed Hajric, who had that blue shirt on and had those papers in his hands that His Honour asked about? So do you remember this individual and the other one next to him carrying papers in his hand? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I remember you showing me the video of these people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe that they were the ones directing the boarding and evacuation? Did you see any members of the Army of Republika Srpska present there or was there only the president of the municipal assembly of Zepa wearing a blue shirt, accompanied by a man with lists in his hand? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, there are two points to make here. The first is that earlier on in the same video, there was in the background a group of what appeared to be soldiers from the Bosnian Serb army. So they were present at the video you have shown me. But, secondly, as I've said previously, you were showing me a video of an event that I was not present at, at that time. I don't know exactly when this video was taken but it is not a video of the evacuation that I stood amongst. So you're showing me two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You had a camera and could have filmed it, and the Prosecution would have showed it then. This is a Prosecution video, not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... any basis at all for the comment that General Tolimir just made. If he has got a basis for that, can he please put it, that if the witness had a camera and could have filmed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We'll show Mr. Gibb's statement later on about the equipment brought in precisely by the members referred to by the witness. Now, if we need to show it now, we can drop this line of questioning for the time being and present it at this stage. I can put this question to the witness right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does he know what sort of equipment his colleague Dibb brought into Zepa illegally or legally? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a camera with you, when you were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not have a camera. I don't remember there being any cameras there. I do remember some video'ing going on at the top of the hill during the meeting between General Smith and General Mladic that preceded my journey down into Zepa that was video'd by the Serbs, by the Bosnian Serbs. But I certainly didn't take a camera down into Zepa myself, and I didn't have a camera, and I'm not aware of any other cameras that might have been down there. And I don't know whether Mr. Dibb had a camera. I would rather doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And my question and the answer of the witness was in relation to -- was in relation to your question, Mr. Tolimir, page 60, lines 13 through 15. You said to the witness: "You had a camera and could have filmed it and the Prosecution would have showed it then." And Mr. Elderkin was asking for a foundation for this statement that this witness had a camera. But we have received an answer now, that he didn't have a camera. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the witness. I said "you" and I meant UNPROFOR representatives. Later on, we'll show a document and a statement wherein Mr. Dibb stated that he was able to bring in special equipment illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us, the frame where you saw the president of the War Presidency of Zepa and other associates of his carrying papers, was it filmed in Zepa or outside of it, in your view, including the evacuation of civilians from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't know, and, therefore, I can't give you a categorical answer. It looks to me as if it was filmed in Zepa but I only went there once -- into the village once in my life, so I can't be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 60 of today's transcript -- sorry. Yeah, page 60, lines 6 and 7, you have stated as follows: "Well there are two points to make here. The first is that earlier on in the same video, there was in the background of what appeared to be soldiers from the Bosnian Serb army." Earlier in the same video, we were looking at another soldier in uniform who you failed to identify. Now, the uniform that was worn by soldiers of the opposite sides how -- how would you be in a position to distinguish between soldiers wearing Bosnian Serb army and soldiers wearing the camouflage from the Muslim army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very good question. And one of the problems in Bosnia at the time is that they all wore, more or less, the same uniform. The reason why I made the distinction in the video that I was shown, and this is the first time I have seen that video that I can recollect, was because the soldiers that I pointed out as soldiers were armed. They were carrying weapons. And whilst you are quite correct, I don't know for certain that they were Bosnian Serb soldiers. I find it highly likely that they were Bosnian Serb soldiers because they were armed and, if not directly supervising the evacuation, they were certainly standing around and accompanying it. So it is a deduction, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. To be fully precise and correct, let's show D112, which is Mr. Dibb's statement. Specifically page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's see exactly what it was that Mr. Dibb said. He didn't refer to filming equipment but to highly sophisticated or sophisticated equipment. Let me quote. We have is on our screen, and the last paragraph on both pages of page 2 reads: "On the 25th of July, I was -- I was woken up at midnight and told that a plan had been created to send a team into Zepa. This was to include Joint Commission Observers, two men: A SAS captain and a staff-sergeant. I was to accompany them. I believe I was chosen to go because of my language skills. Our job was to report back directly to General Smith's HQ exactly what was taking place in Zepa. We had with us sophisticated radio equipment. I do not think that the VRS knew what equipment we had or they may not have let us into Zepa. We were told that we were going to Zepa for two to five days with secure communications to report back to BHC what was happening in Zepa. I was to report through the JCO's Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter and through him to General Smith." This is the reference I made to Mr. Dibb. This is my question: Did you, and I mean your members, when you were in Zepa, were you members of the British Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I -- for the whole of my service, I was a member of the British Army, as were all of my men. The -- the UN Protection Force in Yugoslavia, UNPROFOR, was made up of contingents of different nationalities, soldiers of different nationalities, who were attached to UNPROFOR, seconded to UNPROFOR. They remained members of their own army in that period, but while they were working in Yugoslavia, they were attached to UNPROFOR. So my role there, and the role of my men, was to remain a member of the British Army but be attached to the UN Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To be more precise, I believe we ought to say that you were a member of the British Army, not a member of UNPROFOR. Were you officially a member of UNPROFOR; that is to say, of the international peacekeeping force, or were you primarily a member of the British Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I and my men were officially, and in all practical purposes, seconded to UNPROFOR. We were members of UNPROFOR by any definition you might care to apply. We were also, of course, members of the British Army that we came from and that we returned to. But if you are trying to suggest that we were there as -- we were there and that we were not members of UNPROFOR then that is not correct. We were there and we were members of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was your immediate superior? Who were you subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: My immediate superior was General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he your superior with regard to the British Army or with regard to UNPROFOR? Because each command has its own structure and unit. So what structure did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, as you know, and as you correctly state, each troop-contributing nation has a head of their contribution. And in our case, in the British case, the head of the British contribution to UNPROFOR was for most of my time -- was a guy called Brigadier Pringle, who was based in Gornji Vakuf. He was technically in charge of all military forces who were in Bosnia at the time. However, in practical terms, my -- my boss, my immediately superior was General Smith, because I lived and worked in his headquarters in the residency in Sarajevo and because my role and function, and those of my men, was to support his work in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Had something happened to you in the war, who would have been responsible for that? The Security Council of the UN, the UN command structure, or the British Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: You have to explain what you mean by something happened to me. Do you mean -- what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When serving with the UN, a soldier can suffer any kind of fate, including the worst one. Had something happened to you, who would have provided for your pension to be paid out?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, that's not something I paid much attention to. But my understanding is, and you would perhaps have to get a more expert witness to tell you about the detail of the status of forces agreement between the countries and the UN and so on. But certainly my understanding is that in the event of death or injury of an UNPROFOR soldier, then the troop-contributing nation takes responsibility for his treatment, his care, repatriation of body and so on. But I'm not really an expert in that so you would have to ask somebody who is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt for a moment and put a question. Sir, who was the direct superior of General Smith during that time he served in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, his direct superior, I think, was a French General, called General Janvier, who, I think I'm right in remembering, was based in Zagreb and who had responsibility for all of the forces in the Balkans, I believe. So General Smith, while he was working in Sarajevo, was, if you like, an UN general and had a responsibility through an UN chain of command up to General Janvier and then to, I think, the Security Council. The question that the defendant asked me was in relation to the national command, which was sort of an administrative and legal command, if you like, that went back through heads of forces, back to their own countries and applied to all nations that contributed forces there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us this, Mr. Wood: Could General Janvier issue orders directly to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: To -- issue his orders directly to me? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether he did. I wanted to know whether he could issue orders directly to you; whether General Janvier, who was superior to General Smith, could issue orders directly to you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, you would probably have to ask somebody with a more detailed knowledge of the precise wording of the various status of forces agreements to see what the legal limits on orders were, and I don't know really. Because for practical purposes, all the orders I received were from General Smith and I cannot think of a scenario where General Janvier would have asked me directly to do something. But if there was a scenario where he had a personal requirement to deploy the JCOs into some particular area, then I'm sure what he would have done is told General Smith and General Smith would have told me. But I don't recall that ever happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please: Could someone standing in for General Smith, who otherwise was his subordinate, in General Smith's absence, issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. Because, like any military command structure, there is scope to -- to operate successfully if a particular part of that structure is missing or absent. And if General Smith had been absent on duty or unable to issue orders, then either his deputy who was a French general, called General Gobillard, or his Chief of Staff, who was a Dutch general called General Nicolai, would have given orders. As it is, I can't remember any circumstances when they did give orders to the JCOs, but they could have done so, because they would have been acting in the name of and with the authority of General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether anyone issued an order to you personally by-passing General Smith? Did anyone issue any orders to you, save for General Smith, while you were in Zepa and attending to your other duties?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I need to ask you to clarify. Do you mean anyone within UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Anyone other than General Smith. In practice, did that happen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Nobody in UNPROFOR that I can remember issued me any orders, aside from General Smith. If you want to get into the area of whether there were in the national orders issued to me, then I think that we are moving into an area that I'm not permitted to comment on under Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us whether your stay in Zepa was legal from the standpoint of the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I -- the answer to that question is that I -- I can't comment from the standpoint of the authorities of Republika Srpska. I have no idea what they would regard as legal or illegal. I was there legally as a member of the UNPROFOR under the orders of the UNPROFOR commander, and that is as far as it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you responsible or answerable to any warring party for your actions in the time of war; or are you only answerable to your own command and your own national forces while acting in a territory controlled by the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand your question correctly. Perhaps you could rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will. Do you have any obligations vis-a-vis the side whose territory you used while performing your tasks; or is your only responsibility towards the -- towards those superior to you within your national contingent or those you were directly subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I see. Again, you would have to refer to a more -- to a more expert witness than me to discuss the -- the detail of the status of forces agreements between the various elements here. But from a practical personal perspective, my responsibility was to my commander, and I had no responsibility as such towards any of the warring factions within whose areas we operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that you could stay illegally in the territory of those warring factions, and that even in such a case you wouldn't be called to task to explain your actions to any of the warring factions but only to those you were subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, the details of the agreement by which UNPROFOR was present in the former Yugoslavia are an area you should explore with somebody else. But my understanding of it is that UNPROFOR could go anywhere and do anything for practical reasons without either needing the authority of or being responsible to any of the warring parties. In practice, of course, that simply wasn't possible because many of the warring parties failed to abide by the agreements that had UNPROFOR there in the first place, and so UNPROFOR had very limited freedom of movement in practical terms. But in legal terms, I believe, but I stand to be corrected if somebody more expert can do so -- in legal terms, I believe UNPROFOR could go where it wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Somewhat later, we will show you the agreement on the movement of UNPROFOR across the territory of the warring factions; in this case, the RS. Could we next have 1D614, which is your statement, paragraph 4, on page 2. You provided the statement to the OTP, and it will serve as the basis for my next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have it on the screen first. Yes. Paragraph 4, please. 1D614.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm seeing something on the screen now that appears to refer to an unrelated protected witness and shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It shouldn't be broadcast, indeed. Mr. Tolimir, you should check the right number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My legal assistant is telling me that the number is 613, rather than 614. Thank you, Aleksander. I apologise for having provided the wrong number for e-court. It is 1D613.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this the statement you signed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please, paragraph 4, lines 1 through 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it now in both languages. This part was not redacted: "In Bosnia, I was based in the residency and commanded the JCO teams deployed throughout Bosnia." You stated as much in your statement. My question is this: Why was it called "Joint Commission Observers"? Perhaps you can explain to the Bench why the word "joint" appears.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: The establishment of the Joint Commission Observers preceded my arrival. It had been running for I think six or maybe nine months before I arrived. And my understanding is, remains, that the Joint Commission Observers was set up to provide a verification reporting and facilitation ability to assist the joint commission, which, if I remember correctly, was made up of all parties and surrounded the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement that was signed in, I think, 1994. So the Joint Commission Observers were sort of borne out of that Cessation of Hostilities Agreement as a means of verifying, facilitating and reporting what was going on, so that the agreement might hold together; in fact, of course, it didn't, but the Joint Commission Observers continued after that time. That's my understanding of the origins of the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us for the record who organised it and why it was called joint? Were there a number of forces from a number of countries, or did only the British Army participate in it; that is to say, the special unit of the British air force?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: My understanding is that when it was originally conceived it would be a multi-national force. It was to be a multi-national force; in particular, including the French and the Dutch. The reality was that by the time that I came to command it and it was effectively a British unit, but it was serving as part of UNPROFOR and was, therefore, an UN unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, whether the unit took part in guiding air-strikes, since it was a unit of the special command of the British air force?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: The JCOs were governed by exactly the same rules of engagement as applied to all UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia, and they essentially were that they could uses military force to protect themselves, that was fundamentally the justification. So they had no additional offensive role, if that's what you're trying to imply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they take part in the guiding of the air-strikes? Were they forward air spotters?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Any soldier with a radio can direct an air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you whether you and your men directed any air-strikes; for example, during Operation Srebrenica, or the operation in Zepa? Did you direct air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: During the operation in Srebrenica, there was occasion for my men to call air support in order to safe-guard themselves and those whom it was their duty to protect, and on that occasion they used NATO air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in Zepa, during the operation in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had no men in Zepa prior to the elimination of the -- of the enclave by the Bosnian Serb forces. And, of course, after that, there was no fighting there anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, we must have our second break now, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, we left off when I was asking you if your soldiers in Srebrenica had participated in guiding aviation. Can you give me a direct answer to that question, if you can?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I thought I had given you an answer. Yes, they had in Srebrenica been involved in guiding a NATO air attack, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your repeating that answer. Tell us, were they given the opposite order by the commander of UNPROFOR forces in Srebrenica, his deputy, or somebody from the UNPROFOR HQ in Sarajevo? Or, in fact, who was it who issued the order to them to establish contact with the aviation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: A soldier does not need to be ordered in order to defend himself. They came under threat and they defended themselves. Throughout that action they were in touch with me directly and so if anyone was giving them order, it was me. But they didn't needed to be ordered to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of them go out into the field to search tanks -- Serb tanks in Srebrenica? Were they told by anyone that they had to search and detect tanks and indicate their position? Were they -- these sort of orders given to the soldiers in the field? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, you must remember, as I've stated before, that their job was to report accurately, clearly and in a timely fashion what was going on. So in the case of Srebrenica, they provided minute-by-minute response and information to me -- minute-by-minute response and information to me and what was going on. So to that extent, they obviously were identifying all of the warring factions' forces and reporting their positions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were the one issuing orders, can you tell us where you were located when NATO opened fire on the VRS tanks in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I was in my headquarters in Sarajevo, in the Residency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in the Residency, does that mean you were not a member of UNPROFOR at the time, since you were not billeted in UNPROFOR quarters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I've already made it very clear to you that I was a member of UNPROFOR at that time and all the times I was in Yugoslavia, and I was billeted in UNPROFOR accommodation. In the Residency, as you may remember -- the Residency accommodated probably 150 people of UNPROFOR within its grounds and I stay -- and that's where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, who did you receive orders from to have NATO open fire on the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, I have already stated quite clearly, a soldier does not need to be ordered to defend himself. The soldiers who I had under my command who were in Srebrenica during the period in which the Bosnian Serb army attacked Srebrenica came under fire themselves, and they were fully authorised to use whatever force they required in order to safeguard themselves or those whom its their duty to protect. And they didn't need me to order them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Trial Chamber this: When your soldier is in contact with a plane, is that soldier armed with the same weapons that an aircraft would dispose of, such as rockets, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I think you know the answer to that very well. Most soldiers do not carry around rockets or bombs. A soldier of this sort that I described has a radio through which he can communicate to an aeroplane that is able to deliver weapons carried on aeroplanes, such as rockets and bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell Their Honours then, does that mean that the soldier would have at his disposal all the combat hardware that the particular aircraft is equipped with? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, if you take yourself back to the time in question, you'll recall that UNPROFOR, operating on the ground in Yugoslavia, enjoyed the protection when it required it of the NATO air forces that were based at the time in -- mainly in Italy. So that when and if UNPROFOR needed to utilise air power in order to protect itself or those whom it was its duty to protect, then it had the option of requesting that air support which was then delivered by NATO. So, in a sense, therefore, your question -- or the answer to your question is, did any soldier who has legitimately got reason to call for air support to protect himself or those whom it is his duty to protect has access to whatever weapons systems are available on the NATO aircraft at the time. But, of course, the NATO aircraft at the time are operating to their own rules of engagement, and you have to have a witness here who is familiar with those to tell what they are or they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood. Does this mean that every soldier would independently take decisions as to when a NATO intervention would be warranted because of the actions of any of the sides? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, as I recall there was a process by which UNPROFOR could request the support of NATO in order to protect itself. I was not part of that process because it was a -- a request, I think, that had to be made from General Smith to General Janvier, from General Janvier to Admiral Smith, who was commander of the NATO forces in the area in order to release air support. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let the witness continue with his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just, therefore, going to say that -- that -- that clearly -- clearly you cannot have a situation, and we did not have a situation, where every single soldier can ask for NATO air power whenever they wanted. That is not the case. However, where there was a case for airpower to be released to support UNPROFOR and where that request was made and was accepted and granted, then, as I said earlier on in my evidence, any soldier with a radio can then direct that air power on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that General Smith was in command of NATO, I may have misheard. Who was it who demanded NATO?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No, sorry. There is an understandable confusion there. General Smith was in charge of UNPROFOR and there was an America admiral, called Admiral Smith, who was the -- if I remember correctly, was the senior NATO officer. You are not the only person to be confused by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying the roles that Rupert Smith and Layton Smith played respectively. Is it necessary for the Security Council to approve the use of NATO aviation as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: You're asking the wrong person here. I'm not really familiar with the operations -- or the operating of the Security Council. I've given you my understanding of how it worked at a local level, and you would have to get another witness to describe to you how it worked at the Security Council level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My assistant said that it wasn't properly recorded in the transcript where I said Layton Smith and Rupert Smith. Once we rectify this error in the transcript, tell me, were you subordinated to NATO and I mean your unit, the British contingent, or were you subordinated to someone else in accomplishing missions involving the use of aviation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I repeat what I said before, which is that the unit that I commanded, the Joint Commission Observers, was seconded to UNPROFOR solely. We worked for UNPROFOR, and we operated under the rules of engagement and the legal authority of UNPROFOR only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am told that the transcript doesn't reflect that I said combat use of aviation. My question was: When air power is employed, in that instances, under whose command would your troops be, under NATO or UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: You're making what in English we would say is a mountain out of a mole hill here. The -- as I've said to you very clearly, my soldiers for the entire time they were in Bosnia were under UNPROFOR command and they operated under UNPROFOR's command only, abiding by UNPROFOR's rules of engagement. On occasions when UNPROFOR required to use NATO air to protect itself, then it was necessary for my soldiers, just like any other soldiers to direct NATO air. But, on those occasions, they were still operating as UNPROFOR's soldiers under UNPROFOR's rules of engagement. There is no change in their status just because they happened to be using an air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show D173.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to appear, let me go back to your answer. You didn't answer my question. I didn't ask what the status of soldiers was, but, rather, who they would receive orders from while aviation is used to engage land targets.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, with respect, I think I have answered that question because I have stressed several times now that throughout this period they were operating under UNPROFOR's command and under my command. That did not change at any point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tolimir, indeed, the witness has answered this question in particular several times. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to e-court. I called up the wrong number. We need D137. My apologies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood. What we see here is the transcript entitled: "Srebrenica's Death Fields," a documentary film of Radio Television of Serbia, broadcast on the 9th of July, 2010. Let me direct your attention to third paragraph where it reads: "Hakija Meholjic, member of the Srebrenica War Presidency, 1993 to 1995, in other words during the relevant period of time. "In the meantime, Karremans arrived requesting a meeting. I told him five more minutes so we can first agree amongst ourselves because we have no reason to trust you anymore. We arranged everything, then we received him for talks and he said that NATO had informed him that on the following morning at half past 5.00, a death zone would be set around Srebrenica. Everything that moves about on two, four, or 100 feet, or 100 wheels, one wheel, or on two wheels, that it would be destroyed." This is my question: Was this order issued by someone from UNPROFOR or was it NATO that determined when the death zone would come into effect?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: The simple answer to that is, I don't know. I don't recognise the term "death zone." There were, as you know, some zones that were referred to as safe havens. As to who gave the orders relating to those, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the planes took off from Italy to open fire on the Army of Republika Srpska in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica at the time of the relevant events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether I know where the aeroplanes came from, then, as far as I'm aware, most of them came from air bases in Italy. But I don't know that for a fact. That is just my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the aeroplanes took off from the air bases in Italy in order to carry out the strikes as described by Hakija Meholjic here, who was, in turn, informed about it by Karremans who learned it from NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: You are asking these questions of the wrong person here. I have no knowledge of NATO's orders at the time or the orders given to the aeroplanes at the time. If you want to know that, would you have to call a witness that had knowledge of those things, and I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were your soldier given any sort of task related to the mass scale engagement of aviation in Srebrenica at the relevant time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, what I've said to you already, several times, is that a soldier does not need to be ordered in order to defend himself. My soldiers that I had in Srebrenica came under direct attack from Bosnian Serb forces and they used all the means at their disposal in order to defend themselves, including NATO air. They didn't need orders to do that; that's their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they need as many as 40 aircraft to defend themselves from the attack you referred to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I don't know where you get the figure 40 from. But they needed whatever they needed, in order to defend themselves, whatever that figure was and whatever NATO could provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the paragraph below, it reads: "Hasan Nuhanovic, UN interpreter in Srebrenica." Please look at what he has to say. He speaks of an ultimatum given by the Serb side and then mention is made of some 40 to 70 aircraft. Let's not waste time. Does a single soldier require for his own defence upwards of 40 aircraft? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: You -- you're asking a hypothetical question. It depends entirely on the circumstances. In a scenario where one aeroplane under one bomb will solve the problem, then that's all he needs. In a scenario where a hundred aeroplanes and a hundred bombs are needed to solve the problem, then that is what he needs. There is no fixed answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll put these questions to Mr. Karremans, who was the source of information provided to the Muslim side. Let's look at your statement again. We had it on our screens before. It's 1D613. Thank you. Thank you. Can we show page 3, paragraph 6, lines 1 to 3. Thank you. We have it in both languages. You say: "Near the buses and trucks, I saw seven to eight Serb policemen in paramilitary uniforms lining up people to board the buses." A moment ago, we saw what was the first day of boarding. Did you see in the footage today soldiers lining up civilians and boarding them on the buses? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: In the video you showed me, which, as we've already established, was not the same occasion which I described in my statement, but in the video you showed me, then there were a number of armed men who I believe were Bosnian Serb soldiers. In the video you showed me, they were standing around and watching. However, on the occasion that I described to you, I remember seeing people like that, and I don't know if they're the same people or people like that who were organising and lining up people, women and children, to get onto the buses in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that they were not members of the Army of Republika Srpska since you saw them as you say in paramilitary uniforms, or can you explain Their Honours -- to Their Honours what paramilitary uniforms means?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I have no -- I have no way of telling whether they were formally members of the Bosnian Serb army or the Bosnian Serb police, or any other group. I can't tell that by looking at them. Because as we've already discussed between Their Honours and myself, the uniforms were very similar. It is very difficult to tell. So -- but they were clearly paramilitaries, they were armed. They were, in effect, soldiers, and that -- that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber as a soldier what the hallmarks of a paramilitary uniform would be, since you used the term in your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I use the term, really, to indicate that they were -- that it was a uniform, not necessarily a formal uniform as you would find in a formal army, where everyone dresses the same and looks exactly the same and there's a standard formula for the dress. Paramilitary uniforms, generally speaking, are more informal. For example, they might not wear hats or they might have different coloured T-shirts under their uniform. My uses of the word "paramilitary" was merely to -- to make the point that these were people who were clearly soldiers in one form or another but were not necessarily regular soldiers, formal soldiers in any regular army that I recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing, I see in paragraph 6 of your statement that you are referring to seven to eight Serb policemen in paramilitary uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the reason to classify them as policemen rather than army soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No reason, really, Your Honour. I think I had assumed at the time that they were policemen. I don't know now whether they were policemen or soldiers, and I think the distinction between the two is probably a fairly blurred distinction. I can't be sure that they were policemen, but that's what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you consider the VRS a para-army, a paramilitary, and is that what you meant to say in expressing this view in your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well it's a matter of record that Republika Srpska was an unrecognised state with an unrecognised army. Equally, it is foolish of anyone to pretend there was no army. So they seemed to me to fit quite neatly into the definition of a paramilitary army in the sense that they were not a formal army of a formally recognised state, but they were clearly armed men going about military activity. That is a pretty neat description of a paramilitary force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, tell us what does -- what do the laws of war envisage that different warring parties need to be -- need to wear in times of war? What kind of uniform needs to be worn by, say, international forces and by those present locally?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Again, I don't pretend to be a legal expert on the basis of uniforms in war. The reality is that one expects any military force, and UNPROFOR is an example, the British Army is an example, to wear a recognisable and distinctive uniform and insignia so that it is possible to distinguish friend from foe, combatant from non-combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you used the terminology that was otherwise used by the Muslim side in the war, for their own purposes, did you just now express your own position about the VRS or the Muslim position; or did you rely in your answer on the laws of war, which state that any member of the army needs to bear the insignia of that particular army and that the insignia need to be displayed in open view and that they had to wear specific uniform and use specific weapons? Did you rely on the terminology as can be found in the laws of war or did you put forth your own personal position or the position of the Muslim side, or someone else, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: In all of the evidence I have given, I have given my own personal opinion and my own personal observation of what I saw. In describing the uniform as being paramilitary, whether that term is used by other people or not is, frankly, of no concern to me. My impression of it was that the uniform worn by these people was, if you like, a casual non-standard nature that I recognised as being generally worn by people like Republika Srpska army. I'm not trying to make a big thing about the form of their uniform, and, to be frank, it seems to be something of a diversion, really. But I certainly am not using any terminology or taking any position that is derived from anybody else. I am giving you my opinion and my observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was General Mladic, too, a member of the paramilitary, given the uniform he wore and given the fact that the other members of the army wore the same uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I'm not sure that we're -- that my -- I'm not sure that my opinion as to the legal status of the Bosnian Serb army is very relevant here. But General Mladic was clearly a regular officer of the regular Yugoslavian army, and, generally speaking, he bore himself and wore his uniform and conducted himself in a manner consistent with being a regular officer of a regular army. I'm making a distinction, really, between that sort of conduct and uniform and the sort of conduct and uniform that one finds in less -- in irregular forces or in paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order not to have to go back to the Zepa footage, because we will have ample opportunity to see it with some other witnesses, I'd like to thank you now for having testified here and for having come here. Thank you for all the answers you provided. I wish you a safe journey home and may God bless you. I hope you return home safely in keeping with God's will.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is it, as far as our questions go. I would like to thank all those who assisted us through the process today, and I believe I made a number of mistakes when stating out numbers for e-court. I apologise yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have one last question for you. Let's go back to your description of General Tolimir. On page 8 of today's transcript, lines 11 to 14, you said that he was -- he carried a small grenade at the belt in -- in a -- sort of a pouch, and you said that he told you himself that he would use it against himself if he was captured so that he is not captured alive. So I would just have two questions for you, a few small questions, short questions. Can you please tell me why is it that that detail stayed engraved in your memory? How come you told us about this? What does it mean for you? This gesture, the fact that he was carrying a small grenade in his pocket? Why is that so important for you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: Because it's unusual. I have met many, many, soldiers from many, many, armies all over the world in my military career. I have never met a man before who carries a grenade in his pouch or his pocket ready to kill himself if he's going to be captured. So what it said to me was one of two things: Either General Tolimir was a fanatic and was concerned that he knew things that he didn't want to be revealed were he to be taken alive; or it meant that he was simply - how can I put this politely - somebody who liked living a sort of macho part, if you like, of having such a thing on his belt, so -- and I believed the former instantly. So it seems to me that it said something about the man that he felt that he had to carry a grenade in a pouch at his belt. And I would also point out actually that he was the one that raised it. He -- he pointed it out, if you like, because it was part of -- my deduction is it was part of him establishing himself in our minds as somebody who was important and dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I must say that you've answered to some questions that I wanted to put to you later. I'm just telling you because I wanted to know what logic I was using here. But, in fact, this is what else I wanted to know. Given your military experience, is it usual that armed forces in the country to see a high rank officers to behave this way in the NATO tradition and in the Soviet blocks, according to the Soviet block tradition. But I think you have already answered in a way, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I think so. I mean, I think that there are big cultural differences between the way that the Warsaw Pact generals would conduct themselves, if you like, and the way in which NATO generals, roughly an east/west sort of divide, and typically those ex-Soviet or ex-Warsaw Pact officers that I have had the pleasure to know have tended to be much more rigid, much less independently minded than the NATO officers that I have met. So in that sense, it is understandable that Tolimir should ask questions about who gave orders, et cetera, because in the culture in which he grew up, I would speculate that he is used to people having to have orders before they do things; whereas in the NATO western culture, there is much less requirement to give a specific order for someone to do something, for example, defence themselves, because it is assumed that a soldier of the British Army or the French army or the German army or the Dutch army knows he has got to defend himself, but I can understand where there is a cultural difference there between ex-Warsaw Pact and NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So I would like to know this as well: General Tolimir was afraid to be captured by whom, by the BiH, or by NATO forces or by the UNPROFOR? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: He didn't say. I would be surprised if it was by UNPROFOR because, of course, at the point I'm talking about, UNPROFOR had a very relatively passive role, and I don't think that Tolimir and his colleagues were very frightened of UNPROFOR. So I don't think it was UNPROFOR he was concerned about. It might have well have been the BiH that he was concerned about or it might just have been, if you like, a general unwillingness to be captured. But, I don't know is the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And one last question: Were you convinced by this explanation? Because you knew of the situation and you knew him in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Convinced by the explanation about the grenade or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, because I'm under the impression that there was an exchange in the way that he told you something private, so when he explained to you why he was carrying the grenade, did you believe him, were you convinced that that was the real reason why he had this grenade on him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID JOHN WOOD
utterances.text: No. I think that -- I mean, I didn't sit down and analyse it at the time. But I think that my impression was that it was more an act of bravado than a genuine attempt to make sure that he could be captured. I think it was slightly for show, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elderkin, have you any estimation about the length of the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Very precisely, Your Honour, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is an appreciated answer. Thank you very much. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination. There is no need to stay during the next week in The Hague. You are now free to return to your normal activities, and the Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come here and to provide us with your knowledge. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the Court Usher will assist you leaving the courtroom. But I have to come back for a short oral decision, an urgent decision which both parties need in relation to another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion to convert seven viva voce witnesses to Rule 92 ter witnesses which was filed on the 22nd of February, 2011, and provided to the accused in B/C/S on the 7th of March, 2011. The Chamber notes that one of the seven witnesses referred to in the motion is Witness 187, who is listed on the Prosecution's list of witnesses for the month of March. For this reason, the Chamber will now issue an oral decision pertaining to Witness 187 only. The Chamber heard the position of the accused during the session on Tuesday, the 8th of March, during which Mr. Gajic submitted, inter alia, that the conversion of Witness 187 from viva voce witness to a Rule 92 ter witness would result in a much greater burden on the Defence while preparing for Witness 187's testimony. Although the Chamber acknowledges the Prosecution's effort to reduce the time required for its examination-in-chief of Witness 187, in light of the fact that Witness 187's testimony is now scheduled to occur in the week of 28th of March, in noting the additional preparation which would be necessary for the accused to carry out in a short time-frame, the Chamber is of the view that, in this specific circumstance, the portion of the Prosecution's motion which pertains to Witness 187 should be denied. Witness 187 shall be heard viva voce. This concludes the hearing of today and for the week. We adjourn now and resume next week on Monday in the afternoon, 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of March, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
